steps.title: The Seed Thief Strikes Again!
steps.story: Reza fills his bird feeder every morning, and every morning a clever squirrel climbs up and eats the lot before the birds get a single seed. Reza doesn't want to hurt the squirrel. He just wants the birds to get their breakfast. Can YOU design a feeder that birds can use but a squirrel can't, without hurting anyone?

steps.prompt: Do you already have an idea for letting some visitors in and keeping others out?

steps.intro: How does nature let some visitors in and keep others out? Plants and animals use shape, size and slippery surfaces to choose who gets in. Let's find out how!

clues.text: A pitcher plant has a slippery rim. When it's damp, insects that step on it skid, like a car on a wet road, and can't get a grip.
Some acacia trees have big thorns that give hungry animals a poke. Bullhorn acacias also give ants a home inside their thorns, and the ants chase away animals that try to eat the leaves.
Some flowers hide their sweet nectar at the bottom of a long, thin tube. Only a hummingbird's long beak and tongue can reach it, so bees and other visitors miss out.

A weaver bird builds its nest hanging from the tip of a thin branch, with the entrance at the bottom, sometimes at the end of a long tube. The bird flies straight in, but snakes find it very hard to climb down and inside.

steps.secret: Design a filter! Shape, size and slipperiness can welcome the right visitor and gently stop the wrong one. A small bird weighs about 20 g, can fly and has a thin beak. A squirrel weighs about 500 g, climbs, jumps and has strong paws. Use those differences: a smooth, wobbly dome or cone a squirrel can't grip, small holes only a beak fits, or a perch that sinks and closes under a heavy squirrel. Real squirrel-proof feeders use exactly these tricks.
steps.reveal_hint: What can a bird do that a squirrel can't? How could your feeder use that difference?

steps.instructions: Run the slippery slope test. Tape four surfaces onto a flat board: cardboard, sandpaper, a plastic folder and kitchen foil. Put a rubber eraser, your pretend squirrel paw, at the top of the board and slowly lift one end. Use a protractor to measure the angle when the eraser starts to slide. Record your results: Surface | Angle it slides at.
hints: Lift the board slowly and in the same way each time, so the test is fair. Repeat each surface 3 times and pick the middle result.
The smoother the surface, the lower the angle when the eraser slides. Smooth plastic makes a great slippery shield that can't hurt anyone.

steps.prompt: Draw your feeder from the side, with the pole or string it hangs from.
steps.guidance: Label the squirrel stopper and the bird door. Show how a squirrel would try to get in, and why it can't.

steps.instructions: Build your feeder from a plastic bottle, card, string and plastic plates or bowls. No grease, spikes, glue or spicy powder: nothing that could hurt birds or squirrels. Do the squirrel test: a helper plays the squirrel, using only a toy or a gloved hand, and may only climb up from below or reach down from above. Time how many minutes it takes to reach the seed, and stop at 5 minutes. Then check a pretend beak, like a pencil, can still reach the seed. Ask an adult to help hang it outside, at least 1.5 m high and 3 m away from fences, walls or branches a squirrel could jump from.
test_criteria: For how many minutes did the squirrel test fail to reach the seed?
Can a pretend beak still reach the seed easily?
Improve one thing and test again. Did the squirrel test fail for longer?
hints: Think like the squirrel: where would you grab first? Make that spot smooth, round and wobbly.
Put a wide, smooth, upside-down bowl or plate on the string or pole above or below the feeder, so it tips and spins when grabbed. Squirrels can't hold on, but birds just fly around it.

steps.celebration_text: Tweet tweet! The garden is full of birds having breakfast at last. And the squirrel? Reza put a few nuts on the ground at the far end of the garden, so everyone gets fed, fair and square.
steps.share_prompt: Share a photo of your feeder and your squirrel test time on the Ideas Wall. What did you learn by thinking like a squirrel?

age_tier_variants.summary: Test which surfaces are most slippery, then build a feeder that stops a pretend squirrel for as long as possible while birds can still eat.

age_tier_variants.title_override: Biomimicry: Selective Access and Friendly Barriers
age_tier_variants.summary: Measure friction angles, design a feeder that filters visitors by weight, size and grip, and compare it with pitcher plant rims, hummingbird flowers and weaver bird nests.
